w8-q1: Incorrect — Traditional mobile networks have rigid hardware, not an overly flexible architecture.
Incorrect — Traditional networks lack flexibility and are hard to manage; excess centralized control is not the listed problem.
Incorrect — Traditional mobile networks are cost-expensive, so very low operational cost is not a problem listed.
Correct — Static, over-provisioned networks are inflexible under high-demand mobile traffic, making them hard to scale.
w8-q2: Incorrect — The controller end hosts the Odin master, not the agent.
Incorrect — The Odin agent does not replace OpenFlow; it works alongside it.
Correct — The Odin agent sits at the access points with the physical devices and communicates with the controller.
Incorrect — Billing for cloud resources is unrelated to the Odin agent.
w8-q3: Incorrect — Mobi-Flow places rules based on predicted user location, not randomly.
Correct — Mobi-Flow predicts users' future location and proactively places flow-rules at the access points they may associate with.
Incorrect — Mobi-Flow works with a controller; it does not remove the need for one.
Incorrect — Proactive placement aims to avoid rule misses, not to increase PACKET-IN messages.
w8-q4: Incorrect — CloudSim simulates cloud environments, not wireless software-defined networks.
Incorrect — NS2 is a general network simulator, not the tool named for wired plus IEEE 802.11 SDN experiments.
Incorrect — GreenCloud is a data-center energy simulator, not a wireless SDN tool.
Correct — Mininet-WiFi deploys networks supporting both wired Ethernet and wireless IEEE 802.11 protocols.
w8-q5: Incorrect — NIST describes a shared pool, not fixed dedicated hardware.
Correct — NIST defines cloud as on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources.
Incorrect — The pool includes networks, servers, storage and applications, not only storage.
Incorrect — The pool includes servers, storage and applications too, not only networking.
w8-q6: Correct — Rapid elasticity is a NIST essential characteristic; resources are allocated and released rapidly and automatically.
Incorrect — Cloud allocation is automatic and on demand, not manual.
Incorrect — Cloud uses a shared multi-tenant pool, so single-tenant-only access is not an essential characteristic.
Incorrect — Cloud usage is metered and pay-per-use, so fixed billing regardless of usage does not fit.
w8-q7: Incorrect — A public cloud is available to any person or industry, not one organization.
Correct — A private cloud serves a single organization, managed on-premises or by a third party off-premises.
Incorrect — A community cloud is shared by several organizations with common concerns.
Incorrect — A multi-cloud uses several cloud providers; it is not defined as exclusive to one organization.
w8-q8: Correct — AWS is a public cloud provider, as are Google Compute Engine and Microsoft Azure.
Incorrect — An internal private data center serves one organization, so it is a private cloud, not a public one.
Incorrect — A dedicated server room for one organization is a private set-up, not a public cloud.
Incorrect — A community-only cloud shared by hospitals is a community cloud, not a public cloud.
w8-q9: Incorrect — SaaS delivers finished software applications, not raw infrastructure.
Incorrect — PaaS provides a platform for developers to build applications, not the underlying infrastructure itself.
Correct — IaaS provides basic building blocks: networking, virtual or dedicated computers, storage and operating systems.
Incorrect — DBaaS offers database services, not general computing infrastructure.
w8-q10: Incorrect — A DNS server resolves names; it does not let virtual machines share hardware.
Incorrect — A load balancer distributes traffic across servers; it does not virtualize hardware.
Incorrect — A firewall filters traffic; it does not let virtual machines share physical hardware.
Correct — The hypervisor sits above the physical hardware and manages multiple VMs, each running its own operating system.
w8-q11: Incorrect — IaaS provides infrastructure that the user still manages, unlike the middleware offering described.
Incorrect — SaaS delivers complete software applications to end users, not middleware for developers.
Correct — PaaS is application middleware as a service, removing the need to manage hardware and operating systems.
Incorrect — Community cloud is a deployment model, not a service model.
w8-q12: Incorrect — The data center's physical location is not the primary purpose of an SLA.
Correct — An SLA defines the non-functional requirements expected from the provider, such as quality, utility and warranty of service.
Incorrect — An SLA does not specify the provider's programming language.
Incorrect — An SLA does not list the provider's hardware vendors.
w8-q13: Correct — Service accounting aims to obtain resource usage information, typically as records based on metric measurements.
Incorrect — Service accounting concerns resource usage, not the physical addresses of end-users.
Incorrect — Service accounting does not involve the source code of hosted applications.
Incorrect — The provider's marketing budget is unrelated to service accounting.
w8-q14: Incorrect — Simulators support pre-deployment testing; they do not permanently replace real cloud infrastructure.
Incorrect — Simulators model cloud environments in software and do not manufacture hardware.
Incorrect — Simulators are meant to test at no cost, not to increase billing cost.
Correct — Simulators provide a reliable, scalable and repeatable environment for evaluating performance before deployment.
w8-q15: Incorrect — CloudSim was not developed at Stanford and is not based on Python.
Correct — CloudSim was developed at the CLOUDS Lab, University of Melbourne, in a Java-based environment.
Incorrect — CloudSim was not developed at MIT and is not based on C++.
Incorrect — CloudSim was not developed at IIT Kharagpur and is not based on JavaScript.
